about.title: About the project
about.lead: A playground for playing all {{count}} Katamino challenges by hand and watching, step by step, how a search algorithm solves them.

game.title: The game
game.body: Katamino is a pentomino puzzle: pieces made of 5 squares. In each challenge a set of pieces has to cover a 5-row board exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps. The board size (the "PENTA") is the number of pieces used: the bigger, the harder.

play.title: How to play
play.pick: Click a piece to pick it up and click the board to drop it.
play.rotate: Right-click or R rotates the piece in hand.
play.mirror: E, or dragging the piece, mirrors it.
play.progress: Completed challenges are saved in this browser and show up marked in the list.

solver.title: The solver
solver.body: On any challenge, "Watch the solver" shows a search solving the board step by step, with the strategy you put together.

tech.title: How it was built
tech.body: React, TypeScript and Vite, with no server: everything runs in your browser, and the solver works in a Web Worker so the screen never freezes. Available in English, Portuguese, Spanish and French.

disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
disclaimer.body: An independent, educational project, not affiliated with the creators or publisher of Katamino.

learn.title: How the solver thinks
learn.lead: Solving a Katamino looks simple, until you count how many ways there are to get it wrong. This page shows why the problem is hard, which algorithm the solver uses, and how each criterion helps it reach a solution with fewer attempts.

problem.title: What kind of problem is this?
problem.body: Katamino has only rules: either the pieces cover the whole board or they don't. Any arrangement that obeys all of them is a solution, and none is worth more than another. This kind of problem is called constraint satisfaction or, more precisely, exact cover.
problem.rule1: Every square of the board is covered.
problem.rule3: Every piece is used exactly once.
problem.solutionsCaption: Two solutions to the same challenge ({{label}}). They are different, and both are worth exactly the same.

pieces.title: The pieces
pieces.body: They are the 12 pentominoes: every possible way of joining 5 squares edge to edge. Each one is named after the letter it resembles. By rotating and mirroring, a piece can show up in 1 to 8 different ways, and each way is one more option for the solver to test. Click a piece to see its ways.
pieces.orientations_one: Piece {{piece}} can only be placed {{count}} way
pieces.hint: Symmetric pieces like X and I leave almost no choice; crooked ones like F, L, N, P and Y have eight.

hard.title: Why is it hard?
hard.body: Each piece can go in many places on the board. And the choices multiply: the number of combinations is the product of the options of each piece.
hard.productNote: This counts every way of putting the pieces on the board, even the ones that overlap. It is the size of the haystack the solution is hidden in.
hard.chartTitle: The haystack grows with every piece
hard.chartNote: One example challenge for each board size. The scale is logarithmic: a slightly longer bar stands for a number thousands of times bigger.
hard.time: Testing a million combinations per second, the 12-piece challenge would take about {{years}} years, some {{times}} times the age of the universe. Brute force is not an option: the search needs method.

algorithm.title: The algorithm: depth-first search with backtracking
algorithm.body: The solver uses depth-first search with backtracking, the classic technique for constraint satisfaction problems. It is how you would do the puzzle by hand, only without ever repeating an attempt:
algorithm.step1: Pick an empty square of the board.
algorithm.step2: Put a piece there that fits, without overlapping any other.
algorithm.step3: Move on to the next empty square and repeat.
algorithm.step4: Stuck, nothing fits? Take the last piece back and try the next option.
algorithm.step5: Stop when the board is full (found it!) or when the options run out (there is no solution).
algorithm.treeBody: Each board below is a state of the search. The root is the empty board; each level down is one more piece placed. The solver goes down a branch until it gets stuck, comes back and goes down the next one. The solution is a leaf on the last level.

lab.title: Lab: watch the tree grow
lab.scrollHint: Scroll sideways to see the whole tree. Click a board to find out what happened there.

stats.fewer: {{percent}}% fewer attempts than the plain search ({{base}})
stats.more: {{percent}}% more attempts than the plain search ({{base}}): not every criterion helps on every challenge
stats.same: The same number of attempts as the plain search on this challenge
stats.baseline: This is the plain search, with no criteria. Switch criteria on above and watch the tree shrink.

detail.open: Attempt {{n}}: placed piece {{piece}}. This state is on the path the search is exploring right now.
detail.dead: Attempt {{n}}: placed piece {{piece}}, but no continuation from there led to a solution. The piece was taken back.
detail.pruned: Attempt {{n}}: placed piece {{piece}}, and the criterion "{{criterion}}" saw at once that no solution comes out of it. The whole branch was cut without being explored.
detail.solution: Attempt {{n}}: piece {{piece}}. This state is part of the solution that was found.

criteria.title: The criteria: search less, find the same
criteria.body: The criteria do not change what a solution is. They change how much of the tree has to be walked before reaching one. There are two kinds, and the difference between them matters.

compare.title: The difference between the two kinds
compare.doesOrder: Change the order in which options are tried. Nothing is ruled out, only postponed.
compare.doesPrune: Rule out branches that provably hold no solution.
compare.effectOrder: Can lower or raise them: it depends on the challenge.
compare.effectPrune: Never raise them. At worst, they cut nothing.
compare.priceOrder: A wrong bet sends the search down the bad branches first.
compare.pricePrune: Every check costs time at every step.

criteria.orderBody: They rule nothing out: they only decide what to try first. The bet is to face the hardest part early, so mistakes show up near the root, where undoing is cheap.
criteria.orderBooks: In textbooks: ordering heuristics, such as MRV (minimum remaining values).
criteria.orderCaveatTitle: Ordering is a bet, not a guarantee
criteria.orderCaveatBody: An ordering criterion can be right on one challenge and wrong on another: the lab above has a challenge where "{{criterion}}" makes the search worse. That is why the solver lets you switch each criterion on and off and compare the numbers.
criteria.pruneTitle: Pruning criteria: when to give up early
criteria.pruneBody: They look at the board after each piece and ask: can this still be finished? If the answer is no, the branch is abandoned right there, and all the boards that would come below it are never visited.
criteria.pruneBooks: In textbooks: pruning and forward checking.
criteria.pruneCaveatTitle: Pruning is a guarantee, but it has a price
criteria.pruneCaveatBody: A pruning criterion only abandons branches that hold no solution, so it never makes the search visit more boards than it would without it. What it charges is time: the check runs after every piece placed and, on a small challenge, can cost more than it saves.
criteria.scarceCaption: How many ways each piece has. The ones with the smallest number are tried first.
criteria.mccCaption: Each number is how many placements still cover that square. In reading order the search would start at the first empty square, with {{first}} possible placements; this criterion goes straight to the square that has only {{min}}.
criteria.deadCaption: The piece walled off {{size}} squares at the top. No combination of 5-square pieces fills {{size}}: end of the branch.
criteria.strandedCellCaption: The marked square is still connected to the rest of the board, but none of the pieces left ({{pieces}}) can cover it.
criteria.strandedPieceCaption: There is plenty of room left, but piece {{piece}} no longer fits anywhere. Since every piece must be used, there is no point in going on.

prune.title: Pruning criteria
prune.summary: Give up on a branch early.

base.name: Try, undo, try again
base.summary: Always on: the search everything else builds on.
base.details: Takes the next empty square, tries a piece there and moves on. When it gets stuck, it removes the last piece and tries the next option. On its own it finds a solution eventually, but it only notices a mistake when nothing fits anymore.

scarcePiecesFirst.name: Stiffest pieces first
scarcePiecesFirst.summary: Tries the pieces with the fewest orientations before the flexible ones.
scarcePiecesFirst.details: Pieces like I and X can only be placed in one or two ways; pieces like F and L in eight. Placing the stiff ones while the board is still open avoids discovering late that they no longer fit anywhere.

mostConstrainedCell.name: Hardest square first
mostConstrainedCell.summary: Fills the empty square with the fewest possible placements.
mostConstrainedCell.details: Instead of following reading order, it counts for every empty square how many placements could cover it, and works on the one with the fewest. A square with a single option is a forced move; one with none shows the dead end immediately.

deadRegions.name: Rule out impossible holes
deadRegions.summary: Backs off when an empty area’s size is not a multiple of 5.
deadRegions.details: Every piece covers exactly 5 squares. If a placement walls off an empty area of 3, 7 or 11 squares, no combination of pieces can fill it exactly, so that placement is undone right away instead of being explored.

strandedCells.name: No square left without a way out
strandedCells.summary: Backs off when some empty square can no longer be covered by any remaining piece.
strandedCells.details: After each placement it checks every empty square: is there still a remaining piece that fits over it? If one square has no candidate left, filling the rest is pointless, and the placement is undone.

strandedPieces.name: Every piece still fits
strandedPieces.summary: Backs off when a remaining piece no longer fits anywhere.
strandedPieces.details: After each placement it checks every piece not yet used: is there still room for it somewhere on the board? If one of them fits nowhere, the board can never be completed from here.
